headline: Hidden in Plain Sight: Scientists Name First New Penguin Species in Over a Century
meta_description: Genetic research reveals a previously unknown gentoo penguin species on remote Kerguelen Islands, the first new penguin species formally named since the early…
summary_short: An international team has identified a fourth distinct gentoo penguin species living on the isolated Kerguelen Islands, settling a century-old scientific debate.
body:
On the remote Kerguelen Islands, nearly 2,000 miles from any permanently inhabited landmass, lives a penguin species so genetically distinct that it escaped scientific recognition for generations. An international research team led by scientists from the University of California, Berkeley, and universities in Chile has now formally identified this population as a separate species—the first new penguin species named in more than 100 years. The discovery, published in Communications Biology in September 2026, resolves a debate that has puzzled scientists since the early 1900s: how many gentoo penguin species actually exist?

Genetic sequencing of 64 penguins from 10 breeding colonies across nearly the entire geographic range of gentoo penguins revealed that what researchers long treated as a single, widely distributed species is actually four distinct species. The newly recognized southeastern gentoo penguin, Pygoscelis kerguelensis, looks nearly identical to its relatives—the same white underside and black back—yet its DNA tells a different story. Scientists call this a cryptic species: visually similar to cousins but genetically distinct enough to warrant separate classification.

The discovery carries an urgent environmental message. Three of these four gentoo species face potential threats from warming oceans and climate change reshaping the sub-Antarctic region. As global temperatures rise, suitable penguin habitat on isolated islands could disappear by 2050. Juliana Vianna, senior author and professor at Andrés Bello National University in Chile, emphasizes that conservation institutions across multiple countries—Chile, South Africa, France, the Netherlands, Australia, and New Zealand—must now recognize and protect these distinct species. The gentoo's survival advantage, its flexible diet of fish, krill, and squid, has helped it adapt where narrower-eating relatives struggle. That same adaptability may prove crucial as their island worlds continue to change.
quick_facts: First new penguin species named in over 100 years
Discovered on Kerguelen Islands, 2,000 miles from nearest land
Genetic study of 64 penguins identified four distinct gentoo species
Three newly recognized species threatened by ocean warming and climate change
